image_description: A close-up, side-view of a male duck (drake) floating on water. The image focuses on the rear half of the body, showing detailed plumage textures, the characteristic curled tail feathers, and the blue speculum patch on the wing. The head is partially visible on the far left but mostly out of frame.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Most distinctive feature is the broad, flat bill adapted for filter-feeding; bill is dark grey to yellow-green.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The head and bill are largely outside the frame or obscured by the angle; only the back of the neck/head is visible.
The eye is not visible in this crop/angle.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Body is stocky and compact, streamlined and buoyant with dense waterproof plumage.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The visible portion of the body shows dense, realistic feather texture and a streamlined shape consistent with a floating duck.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Breeding plumage is typically more colorful than female: common patterns include iridescent green head with white neck ring and grey body (mallard), or chestnut head with grey body.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The plumage shows complex patterning with brown mottling on the flanks and a distinct blue speculum patch bordered by white, which is characteristic of male mallards/drakes.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Legs are short and set far back on the body with webbed feet (three forward toes connected by webbing).
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The legs and feet are submerged or hidden beneath the body/water line and are not visible.
The folded wing is visible, showing the correct structure and the blue speculum patch typical of drakes.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Tail is short with curled central tail feathers (drake feathers) in many species.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The central tail feathers are clearly curled upward, a definitive anatomical feature of male ducks.
